statement: As described in one narrative review of reports up to 2014 (Wood et al., 2015), so that its figures are second-hand and come from published case reports and case series (several known only from conference abstracts), one US poison-centre series, cases and deaths reported to European agencies and a news report, none of them appraised: NBOMes (N-2-methoxybenzyl relatives of the 2C phenethylamines, among them 25I-, 25B- and 25C-NBOMe; the review describes 25I-NBOMe as a very potent agonist of the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor) were typically sold on blotters, and also as powder and liquid, and 8 of the 10 first detections of an NBOMe in Europe, from January 2011 to June 2013, were on blotters, alone or with powder (editors' count from the review's table). In several reported cases people believed they had taken LSD: a woman at a US festival had taken 'acid' on blotters whose remains held mainly 25C-NBOMe (her own samples were not tested); three people in Belgium who said they had taken 'synthetic LSD' had 25I-NBOMe, and no other drug, in their urine; and among the deaths, a 21-year-old man in Houston who had taken two 'hits of acid' had 25I-NBOMe, with cannabis metabolites, in post-mortem samples, a person in Belgium had used a blotter they thought held LSD, in which no LSD was found (whether an NBOMe was tested for is not reported), and in Richmond, Virginia, a 19-year-old died while 'trip sitting' friends who were using 'acid' blotters, and an unused blotter from the case held 25I-NBOMe, which was also found in his own samples. How often blotters sold as LSD hold an NBOMe was not measured. In the 29 published poisoning cases (25I-NBOMe 23, 25B-NBOMe 3, 25C-NBOMe 3; aged 14 to 31, and 17 of the 19 whose sex is given were men, editors' count), the review reports a fast heart rate in 96.6%, high blood pressure in 62.0%, agitation or aggression in 48.2%, seizures in 37.9% and a high body temperature in 27.6%, and acute kidney injury in 5 people; these features are not defined, and the review's own case descriptions do not reproduce all of the shares (by the editors' count, seizures in 12 of the 29 and kidney injury in 6), so they are approximate. The severe courses described include continuous seizures (status epilepticus), muscle breakdown with kidney injury treated with dialysis or blood filtration in 3 people, lung injury needing a long period on a ventilator, and 38 days in intensive care for a man who injected a liquid labelled 25I-NBOMe (he left hospital after 43 days with normal kidney function); five of seven men in one English series went home from the emergency department within a day. Published cases favour severe ones: in 25 cases reported to Texas poison centres in 2012–2013 (no other substance reported in 21), seizures were recorded in 4% (1 of 25, editors' calculation), against 38% across the published cases, and the commonest effects were a fast heart rate (52%), agitation or irritability (48%), hallucinations (32%) and high blood pressure (32%). Eight deaths had been reported with 25I-NBOMe (in one with 25C-NBOMe too), and the review's abstract says it was detected in all eight, but its text reports laboratory detection in five (two in Houston, one in Richmond, one in Belgium whose death was reported as due to natural causes, and one in the UK, a 22-year-old man who drowned, with 25C-NBOMe and five other substances also found) and none reported for three (an Australian news report, the Belgian death after a blotter thought to hold LSD, and a Polish death). Several deaths followed disturbed behaviour, such as falls from balconies, or self-injury and aggression before collapse, and the review says the role of NBOMes in the deaths had often not been determined. By the editors' count, the NBOMe was found in the person's own samples in 15 of the 29 published poisoning cases, only in the remaining product in 2, and in no sample linked to the person in 12, and other drugs were found or reported in many cases; the review's authors read the reported features as serotonin toxicity together with stimulant-like (sympathomimetic) toxicity, much like MDMA, some amphetamines and mephedrone. These reports count no one who used an NBOMe without harm, so they cannot give the risk of harm from a use, and no source here compares NBOMes with LSD; in two non-representative 2013 surveys aimed at people who go clubbing (one of them by two of the review's authors), NBOMe use was much less common than LSD or mephedrone use (ever used: 2.6% against 39.4% for LSD among 22,289 respondents of the Global Drugs Survey). Nothing after 2014 is covered. How often people seek emergency treatment after taking LSD is a separate answer. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: What are NBOMes, and are they sold as LSD? NBOMes are lab-made drugs related to the 2C drugs, and they were usually sold on blotters. One review of reports up to 2014, whose figures are second-hand, describes several cases in which people who got sick or died thought they had taken LSD or 'acid'; nobody measured how often blotters sold as LSD hold an NBOMe. In 29 published cases of poisoning, nearly all people had a racing heart, about 6 in 10 high blood pressure, about 4 in 10 seizures and about 3 in 10 a high temperature, and some needed intensive care, a breathing machine or dialysis. Published cases tend to be the worst ones: among 25 cases reported to poison centres in Texas, 4 in 100 had seizures. Eight deaths had been reported with one NBOMe, 25I-NBOMe, and a laboratory found it in five; some of these people had taken other drugs too, and the review says the drug's role in the deaths was often not settled. These reports cannot say how risky one use is, and nobody compared NBOMes with LSD.
population: People with reported poisoning or death after NBOMe use, 2010–2014, as gathered in one narrative review: 29 published poisoning cases (several known only from conference abstracts), 25 cases reported to Texas poison centres in 2012–2013, 25 non-fatal cases reported to the EU Early Warning System, and 8 reported deaths (forensic reports, the EU Early Warning System and a news report); first detections of NBOMes in Europe, 2011–2013
exposure: NBOMe drugs (mostly 25I-NBOMe; also 25B- and 25C-NBOMe), reported by the person or found by laboratory analysis of the person's samples or of the product, often with other drugs; the forms in which they were found or taken (blotters, powder, liquid, capsules), including blotters taken as LSD or 'acid'
comparator: None: case reports and one poison-centre series with no comparison group; the review sets the published cases beside the poison-centre series; no comparison with LSD
outcome: Clinical features, severe complications and deaths as reported, whether the drug was confirmed by laboratory analysis, and cases in which people believed they had taken LSD
magnitude: Wood et al. (2015), second-hand: first detections in Europe 2011–2013, 8 of 10 on blotters (editors' count, Table 1). 29 published poisoning cases (25I 23, 25B 3, 25C 3): tachycardia 96.6%, hypertension 62.0%, agitation/aggression 48.2%, seizures 37.9%, hyperthermia 27.6%, acute kidney injury 5 patients (as printed; editors' count from the case descriptions: seizures 12 of 29, kidney injury 6); NBOMe found in the person's own samples in 15 of 29, product only 2, no linked analysis 12 (editors' count). Texas poison centres 2012–2013, 25 cases: tachycardia 52%, agitation/irritability 48%, hallucinations 32%, hypertension 32%, confusion 24%, mydriasis 20%, seizures 4% (1 of 25, editors' calculation) against 38% in published cases. Deaths: 8 reported with 25I-NBOMe (abstract: detected in all 8); laboratory detection in 5, none reported for 3. Global Drugs Survey 2013 (22,289; non-representative): ever used an NBOMe 2.6%, LSD 39.4%. No denominators of people who used NBOMes; no rates or intervals.

evidence.extracted: Narrative review by two clinical toxicologists in London and two staff of the EU drugs agency (EMCDDA): PubMed searched for 'NBOMe' and the names of ten NBOMe compounds, 1966–2014; abstracts of two clinical toxicology congresses (2010–2014 and 2010–2013); the EU information system and database on new drugs; a Google search for grey literature; each paper kept if it related to prevalence of use or acute toxicity. No other eligibility criteria, selection procedure or appraisal of the reports is described.

Three people in Belgium, brought to hospital from the same party, reported using 'synthetic LSD'; 25I-NBOMe was confirmed in their urine, with no other drugs detected. A 21-year-old man in Houston who reportedly had taken two 'hits of acid' and smoked cannabis hallucinated, reportedly injured himself, attacked a friend, and was found unresponsive; 25I-NBOMe and cannabis metabolites were found in his post-mortem heart blood and urine. A 19-year-old in Richmond, Virginia, 'trip sitting' friends who were reportedly using 'acid', behaved strangely and was found after probably jumping or falling from a balcony; a case-related sample of unused blotter paper held 25I-NBOMe and targeted analysis found it in his blood, urine, brain, liver and bile; his friends did not know he had taken anything, and those who took the 'acid' blotters showed no similar symptoms. In Belgium a person had used a blotter at a party that they thought contained LSD; no LSD was found, and analytical confirmation of 25I-NBOMe was not reported.

evidence.extracted: The abstract says 25I-NBOMe was detected in eight fatalities, in one with 25C-NBOMe, and that its role was not determined in all cases. The text reports analytical detection in five: two people after a rave party in Houston (post-mortem heart blood and urine, with cannabis metabolites; the post-mortem examinations showed only external injuries), a 19-year-old in Richmond (blood, urine, vitreous humour, brain, liver and bile), a man in Belgium whose death was reported as due to natural causes (matrix and method not specified), and a 22-year-old man in the UK who drowned (25I- and 25C-NBOMe, with amphetamine, ketamine, lidocaine, 5-methoxy-diisopropyltryptamine and 2,5-dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine). No analytical confirmation was reported for three: a 17-year-old in Australia known from a media report, who acted erratically and jumped from a third-floor balcony; a Belgian who had used a blotter thought to contain LSD; and a Polish death.

evidence.extracted: No national or international surveys of NBOMe use exist; the only data are two non-representative surveys targeting people who frequent nightclubs. Global Drugs Survey 2013 (22,289 respondents, mainly from the UK and USA): 582 (2.6%) had ever used 25B-, 25C- or 25I-NBOMe; 8,774 (39.4%) had ever used LSD. South East London nightclub survey, 2013 (397 participants): ever used an NBOMe 4.8% against 76.6% for mephedrone; this survey is a congress abstract by Lovett, Measham, Dargan and Wood (reference 19), two of them authors of the review. Two authors are advisers to or members of the UK Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs and the EMCDDA and attended the EMCDDA risk-assessment meeting on 25I-NBOMe; the other two report no declarations.

risk_of_bias.note: Published case reports select severe, unusual or analytically interesting cases (seizures in about 38% of them against 4% in the one poison-centre series); the NBOMe was found in the person's own samples in only 15 of the 29 published cases (editors' count) and other drugs were often present; the features are not defined and the pooled shares cannot all be reproduced from the review's case descriptions; the review is not systematic and does not appraise its sources (card sc_wood_2015: some concerns).

inconsistency.note: The published cases and the poison-centre series differ in how often seizures were recorded, a difference the statement gives and that selection explains; the reports agree on the kind of features.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: the case reports, the poison-centre series and the European reports were not read; everything is as described by one narrative review (METHODS §6.3).

imprecision.note: Counts of reports, not rates; the shares rest on 29 and 25 cases, which the statement gives.

publication_bias.note: The selection of published cases is counted under risk of bias and not twice.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (what was reported, and in which kind of data): starts low as case reports and record series seen through a narrative review; downgraded one level for risk of bias (selected, partly unconfirmed cases, often with other drugs) and one for indirectness (second-hand), bounded at very low; never upgraded. Because every supporting anchor cites one narrative review, the claim stays a draft and its statement says that its figures are second-hand. Status single study: one review; the primary reports it gathers come from different teams but were not read here, so they are not counted as independent replications. The statement gives the review's printed shares, not the editors' recount, and says that they are approximate; it reports deaths with the drug found or reported, not deaths caused by it. Nothing here measures how often blotters sold as LSD hold an NBOMe, the risk of harm from a use, or harm compared with LSD.
